title: Herrera v. Wyoming
lead: Clayvin Herrera invoked a Crow treaty right after Wyoming prosecuted him for elk hunting in Bighorn National Forest. An older judgment against the Tribe threatened to bar that defense, but intervening Supreme Court law changed the basis for treating statehood as the treaty’s endpoint.

actors.name: Crow Tribe
actors.role: Treaty party reserving hunting rights when ceding western land in 1868.

actors.name: Clayvin Herrera
actors.role: Crow member prosecuted for elk hunting in Wyoming.

actors.name: Wyoming
actors.role: State asserting hunting violations and preclusion of the treaty defense.

actors.name: Thomas Ten Bear
actors.role: Individual plaintiff with the Tribe in the earlier Repsis litigation.

actors.name: Justice Alito
actors.role: Dissenter joined by Roberts, Thomas, and Kavanaugh.

proceedings: A Wyoming trial court excluded the treaty defense and convicted Herrera; the state district court affirmed on appeal and the state supreme court declined review. The U.S. Supreme Court vacated and remanded, leaving site-specific occupation, conservation, and an alternative preclusion question unresolved.
limits: The Court did not acquit Herrera or reopen the original Repsis judgment. Its changed-law ruling addressed the statehood ground; the alternative occupation ground’s preclusive effect was expressly reserved. The majority dates the hunting events to 2014, while the dissent begins its investigative account in winter 2013.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Crow reserve hunting rights while ceding a vast territory
sections.cue: Which events did the treaty identify as limits?
paragraphs: In an 1868 treaty, the Crow Tribe ceded more than thirty million acres in what became Montana and Wyoming. Among the United States’ promises was a right to hunt on unoccupied federal lands while game remained and peace continued at the hunting districts’ borders. Negotiations treated continued hunting as central to Crow life.

The treaty did not identify statehood as a termination event. Congress created Wyoming Territory later that year while expressly preserving unextinguished Indian rights. Statehood legislation in 1890 did not mention the hunting right. In 1897, President Cleveland reserved the Bighorn forest lands from entry or settlement.

sections.title: An earlier judgment rejects the treaty claim on two grounds
sections.cue: How did later precedent unsettle part of that judgment?
paragraphs: In Crow Tribe of Indians v. Repsis, the Tribe and Thomas Ten Bear litigated the same treaty right. The Tenth Circuit’s 1995 judgment accepted two independent grounds: Wyoming statehood terminated the right under Ward v. Race Horse, an 1896 Supreme Court decision, and creation of Bighorn National Forest made the land occupied.

In 1999, Minnesota v. Mille Lacs Band of Chippewa Indians addressed a different treaty and rejected reasoning inconsistent with continuing hunting rights after statehood. Whether that decision changed the legal basis of Repsis would become central to Herrera’s later case.

sections.title: Herrera’s prosecution raises the treaty defense again
sections.cue: What did the state courts decide?
paragraphs: Clayvin Herrera, a Crow member living on the Montana reservation, and other members pursued elk into Bighorn National Forest in Wyoming. Wyoming charged him with taking elk out of season or without a state license and being an accessory. The majority placed the events in 2014; Alito’s dissent began its investigation account in winter 2013 and additionally described trophy photographs, carcasses with substantial meat left behind, and Herrera’s admission. The writings did not supply a single reconciled chronology.

The trial court rejected the treaty defense before trial and did not permit its presentation to the jury. Conviction brought a suspended jail sentence, a fine, and a three-year suspension of hunting privileges.

The Wyoming district court, serving as the appellate court, affirmed. It rejected the claim that Mille Lacs repudiated Race Horse, treated Repsis as binding Herrera through his membership in the Tribe, and also considered the forest occupied. The Wyoming Supreme Court declined review. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari from the state district court judgment.

sections.title: The majority finds the statehood rationale fundamentally changed
sections.cue: Why could the earlier determination no longer bar this issue?
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor wrote for Justices Ginsburg, Breyer, Kagan, and Gorsuch. Race Horse had reasoned both that equal-footing statehood conflicted with special hunting rights and that a temporary treaty right was not meant to survive admission. Mille Lacs undermined both: treaty rights could coexist with state sovereignty because necessary, reasonable, nondiscriminatory conservation rules could apply, and abrogation required clear congressional intent or a treaty-specified endpoint. Calling rights temporary did not insert statehood.

Mille Lacs had not expressly overruled Race Horse, but the majority found the reasoning irreconcilable and formally repudiated implied extinguishment at statehood. Repsis had been obliged to follow Race Horse and could not anticipate that shift.

Issue preclusion ordinarily bound actually litigated, resolved, essential issues in a valid judgment. Bies, Limbach, Sunnen, Montana, and Restatement principles recognized an exception for an intervening change in the governing legal context. This was no slight atmospheric change or conflicting lower-court view; the statehood holding’s foundation had fallen.

The Court did not reopen Repsis or destabilize all final judgments whenever precedent changed. It limited use of that determination in Herrera’s distinct case. Compelling reliance or repose might matter elsewhere, but Wyoming identified neither convincingly: conservation regulation remained possible, and the right concerned unoccupied federal land, not private property.

sections.title: Neither statehood nor national-forest designation automatically ends the treaty right
sections.cue: How did the Court understand occupation?
paragraphs: The Statehood Act showed no clear congressional decision to abrogate. The treaty identified occupation, loss of federal ownership, disappearance of game, and loss of peace as limits. Statehood was absent even though future western admissions were foreseeable during negotiations. Wyoming could not substitute statehood for a supposed general end of the frontier.

Occupation had to be understood as the Crow naturally would have understood it. The treaty’s contrast between hunting districts and settlement, its other language, and negotiations pointed to non-Indian residence or settlement. Reserving land from settlement did not itself produce settlement. Federal control and regulation were not synonymous with occupation, and mining and logging evidence did not show the entire forest occupied.

Wyoming could still show that the particular hunting location was occupied or pursue necessary conservation regulation. The trial court addressed conservation, but the appellate court had not, and the Supreme Court did not resolve its viability.

sections.title: The majority reserves the alternative ground’s preclusive effect
sections.cue: Why did the treaty ruling not resolve every obstacle?
paragraphs: The Court expressly did not decide whether Repsis’s independent occupied-land holding precluded Herrera. It read the judgment below as applying preclusion to statehood alone, considered the alternative question outside the grant, and noted unresolved gateways such as full and fair litigation and possible forfeiture.
Thus the changed-law exception defeated this use of the statehood ruling, not categorically every possible preclusive consequence of Repsis.

sections.title: Alito would apply preclusion before reaching treaty interpretation
sections.cue: Why did the dissent find the occupation ruling decisive?
paragraphs: Justice Alito, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas and Kavanaugh, regarded Repsis as settling the Tribe’s right in Bighorn and binding Herrera even though he was not an individual plaintiff. He read the state court as invoking the whole judgment and criticized the majority’s narrower issue definition.

Alito doubted whether Mille Lacs changed the law sufficiently. It clearly rejected equal-footing reasoning but could be read as distinguishing Race Horse’s separate temporary-right ground. He distinguished the majority’s preclusion and tax precedents and warned against sacrificing finality. He ultimately did not need to settle that dispute because occupation independently supported Repsis.

He favored preclusive effect for both independently sufficient grounds, as the First Restatement recommended rather than the Second. Courts could carefully consider alternatives, and concerns about an unappealed weaker ground did not undermine this extensively briefed occupation issue in an action intended to declare legal rights.

sections.title: The dissent also rejects a categorical civil-to-criminal preclusion bar
sections.cue: What remedy did the Court actually choose?
paragraphs: Alito reasoned that declaratory litigation let parties establish rights without first risking prosecution, and finality should bind the loser as well as protect the winner. Civil appellate review had been available and used in Repsis, unlike an unreviewable criminal acquittal. He distinguished preclusion of an offense element from the treaty affirmative defense under Wyoming’s burden framework. Those were dissenting positions, not majority resolutions of the broader issues.

On May 20, 2019, the Supreme Court vacated the Wyoming district court judgment and remanded, 5–4. Statehood did not extinguish the right, and forest designation did not categorically occupy the land. Herrera was not acquitted. Specific-site occupation, conservation, and the reserved alternative preclusion issue could still require attention below.
